# How OpenAI Tools Are Changing Work in Three Very Different Industries

> **In short:** OpenAI says a financial firm, a major US grocery chain, and small business support centers use its AI tools to speed up real work — one cut a 30-minute task to under 4 minutes, and a new partnership will bring AI training to small business owners.

When you hear "AI in the workplace," it's easy to picture the same story every time: a tech company, a software team, lots of code. Three recent OpenAI announcements tell a much wider story.

## A financial firm that trimmed a 30-minute task to under 4

Chatham Financial, which helps companies manage financial risk, says it uses **Codex** (OpenAI's coding-focused AI assistant) along with OpenAI's models to build internal tools and rethink its workflows. According to OpenAI's announcement, the most striking result: a trade validation process that used to take 30 minutes now finishes in under 4.

"Trade validation" means checking that a financial deal meets all the rules and matches the numbers — detail-heavy work where one wrong digit matters. **APIs** (think of them as the messaging channels that let different software programs talk to each other) let Chatham plug OpenAI's models directly into its own systems, so the AI can do the checking work without a human typing prompts.

The takeaway: the biggest time savings come when AI is connected to your existing software, not when you just type questions into a chatbot.

## A grocery chain making shopping easier

Albertsons Companies, one of the largest US grocery operators, says it uses **ChatGPT Enterprise** (the workplace version of ChatGPT, with extra privacy and admin controls) and the **OpenAI API** to help its teams work faster and improve the shopping experience for millions of customers.

The exact uses aren't spelled out in the announcement, but the pattern is familiar: when a large organization has thousands of employees writing reports, summarizing meetings, or analyzing data, an AI assistant can take a lot of that load.

## Small businesses getting real help, not just hype

The third announcement may matter most to everyday readers. OpenAI says it is partnering with America's **SBDC** (Small Business Development Center — a US network of local offices that give free advice and training to small business owners) to expand hands-on AI training and local support. OpenAI has not given a public rollout date for this partnership.

SBDCs exist in most US communities and offer free services. If you run a small business, a side hustle, or freelance, your local SBDC is worth a call today to ask what AI help is available now — you don't have to wait for the OpenAI program to find out what's already there.

## What this means for you

- **If you work at a large company**: Check whether your employer has rolled out ChatGPT Enterprise or a similar tool. Many companies have — and may not have told every team yet.
- **If you run a small business or freelance**: Call your local SBDC today and ask what AI training or support is available now. The OpenAI partnership is rolling out gradually, but SBDCs already help with tech tools — you don't have to wait for it.
- **If you're worried about AI taking jobs**: All three stories describe AI helping people do existing work faster, not replacing entire roles. The pattern that keeps showing up is "humans + AI" doing more than either could alone.
- **If you already use it**: The Chatham example is worth studying. The biggest gains didn't come from typing prompts — they came from connecting AI to existing systems through APIs. That's a step beyond casual use, and it's where the time savings really start to compound.

## Wrap-up

The common thread across a financial firm, a grocery chain, and a small business support network is simple: AI tools are most useful when they're applied to a specific, real workflow. None of these stories started with "let's use AI." They started with a 30-minute task, a busy team, or a small business owner who needed help — and AI turned out to be the right tool for the job. If you have a task that's eating your week, that might be a good place to start.
